text: Where is the headquarters of the United Nations located?
explanation: The UN's main headquarters is located in New York City, United States.

text: The UN Charter was signed at a conference held in which city in 1945?
explanation: The UN Charter was signed on 26 June 1945 at the San Francisco Conference.

text: How many permanent members does the UN Security Council have?
explanation: The Security Council has five permanent members: the United States, United Kingdom, France, Russia and China.

text: What is the total number of member states on the UN Security Council?
explanation: The Security Council has 15 members in total: 5 permanent members and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms.

text: The International Court of Justice is seated in which city?
explanation: The ICJ, the principal judicial organ of the UN, sits at the Peace Palace in The Hague.

text: UNESCO, headquartered in Paris, primarily promotes international cooperation in which fields?
explanation: UNESCO's mandate covers education, natural and social sciences, culture, and communication.

text: In which year was UNESCO established?
explanation: UNESCO's constitution was adopted in London in November 1945, the year of its founding.

text: The World Health Organization is headquartered in which city?
explanation: WHO, the UN's public health agency, is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland.

text: In which year was the World Health Organization established?
explanation: WHO's constitution came into force on 7 April 1948, now observed annually as World Health Day.

text: In which year was UNICEF established to assist children after the Second World War?
explanation: The UN General Assembly created UNICEF in December 1946 to provide relief to children in war-affected countries.

text: Where is UNICEF headquartered?
explanation: UNICEF's headquarters is located in New York City.

text: The UNHCR is the UN agency mandated to protect and assist which group of people?
explanation: The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees works to protect and assist refugees and displaced persons worldwide.

text: In which year was the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees established?
explanation: UNHCR was established by the UN General Assembly in December 1950.

text: Which UN specialized agency, headquartered in Geneva, was founded in 1919 and is the oldest of its kind?
explanation: The International Labour Organization was founded in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles, making it the oldest specialized agency associated with the UN.

text: The International Atomic Energy Agency, established in 1957, is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The IAEA, the world's centre for nuclear cooperation, is headquartered in Vienna, Austria.

text: The Food and Agriculture Organization is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The FAO, established in 1945 to lead efforts against hunger, is headquartered in Rome.

text: Which international organization, founded in 1874 and headquartered in Bern, is considered the oldest international organization still in existence?
explanation: The Universal Postal Union was established by the Treaty of Bern in 1874, predating the ILO and ITU as a formal permanent international body.

text: How many official languages does the United Nations have?
explanation: The UN has six official languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish.

text: In the UN General Assembly, how many votes does each member state hold?
explanation: Under the principle of sovereign equality, every UN member state has exactly one vote in the General Assembly.

text: In which year was the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) established?
explanation: SAARC was founded on 8 December 1985 in Dhaka.

text: Where is the secretariat of SAARC located?
explanation: The SAARC Secretariat has been based in Kathmandu, Nepal, since 1987.

text: How many member states does SAARC currently have?
explanation: SAARC has eight member states after Afghanistan joined in 2007: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.

text: In which year was the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) established?
explanation: The OIC was founded in 1969 following the Rabat Summit.

text: Where is the headquarters of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation located?
explanation: The OIC's headquarters is in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, pending the liberation of Jerusalem.

text: The Economic Cooperation Organization, headquartered in Tehran, was founded in 1985 by Iran, Pakistan and which other country?
explanation: ECO was formed in 1985 by Iran, Pakistan and Turkey, building on the earlier Regional Cooperation for Development.

text: The secretariat of ASEAN is located in which city?
explanation: The ASEAN Secretariat is headquartered in Jakarta, Indonesia.

text: Where is the headquarters of NATO located?
explanation: NATO's headquarters has been located in Brussels, Belgium, since 1967.

text: The main institutions of the European Union are headquartered in which city?
explanation: Brussels hosts the main EU institutions, including the European Commission and the Council of the EU.

text: The African Union, headquartered in Addis Ababa, was established in 2002 as the successor to which organization?
explanation: The African Union replaced the Organisation of African Unity, which had been founded in 1963.

text: The Commonwealth of Nations secretariat is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The Commonwealth Secretariat is based at Marlborough House in London.

text: In which year was the League of Arab States founded?
explanation: The Arab League was founded in Cairo in March 1945.

text: The League of Arab States is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The Arab League's headquarters is located in Cairo, Egypt.

text: In which year was the Gulf Cooperation Council established?
explanation: The GCC was established in 1981 by Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE and Oman.

text: The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation was established in which year?
explanation: The SCO was founded in Shanghai in 2001 by China, Russia and four Central Asian states.

text: The Organization of American States is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The OAS, founded in 1948, is headquartered in Washington D.C.

text: In which year was the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) founded?
explanation: OPEC was founded in Baghdad in September 1960.

text: OPEC is headquartered in which city?
explanation: OPEC's headquarters moved to Vienna, Austria, in 1965.

text: The International Monetary Fund is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The IMF is headquartered in Washington D.C., alongside the World Bank.

text: The IMF was established following which 1944 conference?
explanation: The IMF and World Bank were both created at the 1944 Bretton Woods Conference in New Hampshire, USA.

text: The World Bank is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The World Bank Group's headquarters is in Washington D.C.

text: In which year was the World Bank established?
explanation: The World Bank was established in 1944 at the Bretton Woods Conference, alongside the IMF.

text: The World Trade Organization is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The WTO is headquartered in Geneva, Switzerland.

text: In which year did the World Trade Organization come into existence?
explanation: The WTO was established on 1 January 1995, replacing the earlier GATT framework.

text: The WTO succeeded which earlier trade agreement, signed in 1947?
options: General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade
explanation: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT), signed in 1947, was the predecessor framework that the WTO replaced in 1995.

text: The Asian Development Bank is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The Asian Development Bank is headquartered in Manila, Philippines.

text: In which year was the Asian Development Bank established?
explanation: The ADB was established in 1966 to promote economic development in Asia and the Pacific.

text: The Bank for International Settlements, considered the world's oldest international financial institution, is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The BIS, founded in 1930, is headquartered in Basel, Switzerland.

text: The Islamic Development Bank is headquartered in which city?
explanation: The Islamic Development Bank is headquartered in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

text: The Geneva Conventions primarily deal with which subject?
explanation: The Geneva Conventions form the core of international humanitarian law, setting standards for the treatment of the wounded, prisoners and civilians in war.

text: The four Geneva Conventions, forming the core of international humanitarian law, were adopted in which year?
explanation: The four Geneva Conventions were adopted in 1949, updating earlier conventions dating back to 1864.

text: The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) was opened for signature in which year?
explanation: The NPT was opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in 1970.

text: The Non-Proliferation Treaty is primarily concerned with preventing the spread of which weapons?
explanation: The NPT aims to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons and weapons technology.

text: The Kyoto Protocol, adopted in 1997, primarily commits countries to reduce which type of emissions?
explanation: The Kyoto Protocol set binding targets for industrialized countries to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

text: The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in which country?
explanation: The Kyoto Protocol was adopted in Kyoto, Japan, in December 1997.

text: The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015, is an international treaty primarily addressing which issue?
explanation: The Paris Agreement is a legally binding international treaty on climate change mitigation and adaptation.

text: The Paris Agreement was adopted at which UN climate conference?
explanation: The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21, held in Paris in December 2015.

text: The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, which codifies rules on diplomatic immunity, was adopted in which year?
explanation: The Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations was adopted in 1961 and remains the basis of modern diplomatic law.

text: The Peace of Westphalia, signed in 1648, is widely regarded as the origin of which modern concept?
explanation: The Peace of Westphalia ended the Thirty Years' War and is credited with establishing the principle of state sovereignty that underpins the modern international system.

text: The Treaty of Versailles, signed in 1919, formally ended which war?
explanation: The Treaty of Versailles formally ended the state of war between Germany and the Allied Powers after the First World War.

text: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the UN General Assembly in which year?
explanation: The UDHR was adopted by the UN General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948.

text: The Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty was opened for signature in which year?
explanation: The CTBT, which bans all nuclear explosions, was opened for signature in 1996.

text: The Montreal Protocol, adopted in 1987, is an international treaty designed to protect which part of the environment?
explanation: The Montreal Protocol phases out substances responsible for depleting the ozone layer.

text: UNCLOS, adopted in 1982, is the principal international treaty governing which domain?
explanation: The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea establishes the legal framework for maritime zones, navigation and resource rights.

text: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, often called the 'treaty on treaties,' was adopted in which year?
explanation: The Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties was adopted in 1969 and governs how treaties between states are made and interpreted.

text: The Simla Agreement of 1972 was signed between Pakistan and which country?
explanation: The Simla Agreement was signed between Pakistan and India in July 1972 following the 1971 war.

text: The Tashkent Declaration of 1966 was signed by India and Pakistan following mediation by which country?
explanation: The Tashkent Declaration was mediated by the Soviet Union after the 1965 India-Pakistan war.

text: The Indus Waters Treaty of 1960 between India and Pakistan was brokered with the help of which institution?
explanation: The World Bank facilitated negotiations and is a signatory guarantor of the Indus Waters Treaty.

text: The Camp David Accords of 1978 led to a peace treaty between Egypt and which country?
explanation: The Camp David Accords, brokered by US President Jimmy Carter, led to the 1979 Egypt-Israel peace treaty.

text: The 1988 Geneva Accords primarily addressed the withdrawal of Soviet troops from which country?
explanation: The Geneva Accords, signed by Afghanistan, Pakistan, the US and the USSR, set the terms for Soviet troop withdrawal from Afghanistan.

text: The Treaty of Lisbon, which reformed the institutional structure of the European Union, was signed in which year?
explanation: The Treaty of Lisbon was signed in 2007 and entered into force in 2009.

text: The Maastricht Treaty, signed in 1992, formally established which organization?
explanation: The Maastricht Treaty created the European Union, replacing the earlier European Economic Community framework.

text: The Schengen Agreement, signed in 1985, primarily allows for which of the following among participating European states?
options: Free movement without internal border checks
explanation: The Schengen Agreement abolished internal border checks among signatory states, allowing free movement of people.

text: The Chemical Weapons Convention is overseen by an organization headquartered in which city?
explanation: The Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, which implements the Chemical Weapons Convention, is headquartered in The Hague.

text: The Biological Weapons Convention, the first multilateral treaty banning an entire category of weapons, opened for signature in which year?
explanation: The Biological Weapons Convention opened for signature in 1972 and entered into force in 1975.

text: The Rome Statute, adopted in 1998, established which international judicial body?
explanation: The Rome Statute established the International Criminal Court, which began operating in 2002.

text: The Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 committed signatory states to renounce which of the following?
options: War as an instrument of national policy
explanation: The Kellogg-Briand Pact bound its signatories to renounce war as a means of resolving disputes.

text: The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 establishes the basic legal framework governing which domain?
explanation: The Outer Space Treaty of 1967 forms the basis of international space law, including the principle that space shall not be subject to national appropriation.

text: What is the capital of Kenya?
explanation: Nairobi has been the capital of Kenya since independence in 1963 and is its largest city.

text: What is the capital of Nigeria?
explanation: Abuja replaced Lagos as Nigeria's capital in 1991; Lagos remains the country's largest commercial city.

text: What is the capital of Ghana?
explanation: Accra, on Ghana's Atlantic coast, has served as the national capital since independence in 1957.

text: What is the capital of Ethiopia?
explanation: Addis Ababa is Ethiopia's capital and also hosts the headquarters of the African Union.

text: What is the capital of Mozambique?
explanation: Maputo, formerly known as Lourenco Marques, is the capital and largest city of Mozambique.

text: What is the capital of Senegal?
explanation: Dakar, located on the Cap-Vert peninsula, is the capital of Senegal and its main Atlantic port.

text: What is the capital of Zambia?
explanation: Lusaka has been Zambia's capital since 1935, before independence, and remains its largest city.

text: What is the capital of Zimbabwe?
explanation: Harare, formerly called Salisbury, is the capital and largest city of Zimbabwe.

text: What is the capital of Uganda?
explanation: Kampala is Uganda's capital, while nearby Entebbe hosts the country's main international airport.

text: What is the capital of Morocco?
explanation: Rabat is Morocco's political capital, whereas Casablanca is its largest city and commercial hub.

text: What is the capital of Vietnam?
explanation: Hanoi is the capital of Vietnam, while Ho Chi Minh City is its largest and most populous city.

text: What is the capital of Thailand?
explanation: Bangkok has been the capital of Thailand since 1782 and is the country's political and commercial centre.

text: What is the capital of Malaysia?
explanation: Kuala Lumpur is the constitutional capital of Malaysia, while Putrajaya serves as the federal administrative centre.

text: What is the capital of the Philippines?
explanation: Manila is the capital of the Philippines and sits within the wider Metro Manila urban area.

text: What is the capital of Mongolia?
explanation: Ulaanbaatar is Mongolia's capital and by far its largest city, home to nearly half the national population.

text: What is the current capital of Kazakhstan?
explanation: The Kazakh capital was renamed Astana in September 2022, reverting from its earlier name, Nur-Sultan.

text: What is the capital of Uzbekistan?
explanation: Tashkent is the capital of Uzbekistan, while Samarkand and Bukhara are historic Silk Road cities in the country.

text: What is the capital of Jordan?
explanation: Amman is the capital and largest city of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan.

text: What is the capital of Iraq?
explanation: Baghdad, on the Tigris River, is the capital of Iraq and one of the historic centres of the Islamic world.

text: What is the capital of Nepal?
explanation: Kathmandu is the capital of Nepal, situated in the Kathmandu Valley in the country's hill region.

text: What is the capital of Portugal?
explanation: Lisbon, on the Atlantic coast, has been the capital of Portugal since the mid-13th century.

text: What is the capital of Greece?
explanation: Athens is the capital of Greece and one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world.

text: What is the capital of Austria?
explanation: Vienna is Austria's capital and its largest city, long a centre of European music and diplomacy.

text: What is the capital of Poland?
explanation: Warsaw has been the capital of Poland since 1596 and remains the country's largest city today.

text: What is the capital of Hungary?
explanation: Budapest, formed by the union of Buda and Pest on the Danube, is the capital of Hungary.

text: What is the capital of Norway?
explanation: Oslo is the capital of Norway and its largest city, located at the head of the Oslofjord.

text: What is the capital of Finland?
explanation: Helsinki, on the Gulf of Finland, is the capital and largest city of Finland.

text: What is the capital of Croatia?
explanation: Zagreb, in the country's continental north, is the capital and largest city of Croatia.

text: What is the capital of Canada?
explanation: Ottawa is Canada's capital, chosen by Queen Victoria in 1857; Toronto is the country's largest city.

text: What is the capital of Brazil?
explanation: Brasilia, a purpose-built city, became Brazil's capital in 1960, replacing Rio de Janeiro.

text: What is the capital of Argentina?
explanation: Buenos Aires, on the Rio de la Plata, is the capital and largest city of Argentina.

text: What is the capital of Peru?
explanation: Lima, founded by Spanish conquistadors in 1535, is the capital and largest city of Peru.

text: What is the capital of Colombia?
explanation: Bogota, high in the Andes, is the capital and largest city of Colombia.

text: What is the capital of Chile?
explanation: Santiago is the capital of Chile, while Valparaiso serves as the seat of the national congress.

text: What is the capital of Cuba?
explanation: Havana is the capital of Cuba and its largest city and principal port.

text: What is the capital of Australia?
explanation: Canberra was purpose-built as a compromise capital between Sydney and Melbourne and has served as Australia's capital since 1927.

text: What is the capital of New Zealand?
explanation: Wellington has been New Zealand's capital since 1865, while Auckland is the country's largest city.

text: What is the capital of Fiji?
explanation: Suva, on the island of Viti Levu, is the capital and largest city of Fiji.

text: What is the capital of Jamaica?
explanation: Kingston has been the capital of Jamaica since 1872 and is the largest English-speaking city in the Caribbean.

text: What is the capital of Papua New Guinea?
explanation: Port Moresby, on the southern coast, is the capital and largest city of Papua New Guinea.

text: Which currency is used in Japan?
explanation: The yen has been Japan's official currency since 1871.

text: Which currency is used in South Korea?
explanation: The South Korean won is the official currency of the Republic of Korea.

text: Which currency is used in China?
explanation: China's official currency is the renminbi, whose basic unit is the yuan.

text: Which currency is used in Thailand?
explanation: The baht has been Thailand's official currency for centuries and remains in use today.

text: Which currency is used in Vietnam?
explanation: The dong is the official currency of Vietnam, issued by the State Bank of Vietnam.

text: Which currency is used in Indonesia?
explanation: The rupiah is Indonesia's official currency, issued by Bank Indonesia.

text: Which currency is used in India?
explanation: The Indian rupee is the official currency of the Republic of India.

text: Which currency is used in Turkey?
explanation: The Turkish lira is the official currency of Turkey, issued by the Central Bank of the Republic of Turkey.

text: Which currency is used in Egypt?
explanation: The Egyptian pound has been the country's official currency since the early 20th century.

text: Which currency is used in Saudi Arabia?
explanation: The Saudi riyal is the official currency of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

text: Which currency is used in Israel?
explanation: The New Israeli Shekel is the official currency of Israel.

text: Which currency is used in Iran?
explanation: The Iranian rial is the official currency of Iran, issued by the Central Bank of Iran.

text: Which currency is used in Russia?
explanation: The ruble has been the currency of Russia for centuries and is issued by the Bank of Russia.

text: Which currency is used in Poland?
explanation: The zloty is Poland's official currency; Poland has not adopted the euro despite being an EU member.

text: Which currency is used in Sweden?
explanation: The Swedish krona is Sweden's official currency; like Poland, Sweden has kept its own currency outside the eurozone.

text: Which currency is used in Switzerland?
explanation: The Swiss franc is the official currency of Switzerland and is also used in Liechtenstein.

text: Which currency is used in South Africa?
explanation: The rand has been South Africa's official currency since 1961.

text: Which currency is used in Nigeria?
explanation: The naira is Nigeria's official currency, introduced in 1973.

text: Which currency is used in Kenya?
explanation: The Kenyan shilling is the official currency of Kenya, issued by the Central Bank of Kenya.

text: Which currency is used in Ghana?
explanation: The cedi is Ghana's official currency, first introduced in 1965.

text: Which currency is used in Ethiopia?
explanation: The birr is the official currency of Ethiopia, issued by the National Bank of Ethiopia.

text: Which currency is used in Mexico?
explanation: The Mexican peso is the official currency of Mexico.

text: Which currency is used in Brazil?
explanation: The Brazilian real has been the country's official currency since 1994.

text: Which currency is used in Argentina?
explanation: The Argentine peso is the official currency of Argentina.

text: Which currency is used in Canada?
explanation: The Canadian dollar is Canada's official currency, distinct from the US dollar despite the shared name.

text: Which currency does Ecuador officially use?
explanation: Ecuador abandoned its own currency, the sucre, and adopted the US dollar as legal tender in 2000.

text: What is the name of Panama's official currency, which is pegged 1:1 to the US dollar?
explanation: The balboa is Panama's official currency; it circulates alongside, and is fixed at par with, the US dollar.

text: Which currency is used in Cote d'Ivoire (Ivory Coast)?
explanation: Cote d'Ivoire uses the West African CFA franc, a shared currency used by several former French West African colonies.

text: Which currency is used in Norway?
explanation: The Norwegian krone is Norway's official currency; Norway is not a member of the European Union.

text: Which currency is used in Morocco?
explanation: The Moroccan dirham is the official currency of Morocco.

text: What is the official language of Brazil?
explanation: Portuguese is Brazil's official language, a legacy of Portuguese colonial rule; Brazil is the largest Portuguese-speaking country in the world.

text: What is the most widely spoken language in Mexico?
explanation: Spanish is the dominant language of Mexico, spoken by the vast majority of its population, alongside dozens of indigenous languages.

text: What is the official language of Egypt?
explanation: Arabic is the official language of Egypt, spoken by the great majority of its population.

text: What is the official language of Iran?
explanation: Persian, also called Farsi, is the official language of Iran.

text: What is the official language of Turkey?
explanation: Turkish is the official language of Turkey and is written in the Latin alphabet since a 1928 reform.

text: What is the official language of Indonesia?
explanation: Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia), a standardised form of Malay, is Indonesia's official national language.

text: What is the official language of Mongolia?
explanation: Mongolian is the official language of Mongolia and is written using the Cyrillic script domestically.

text: What is the official language of Vietnam?
explanation: Vietnamese is the official language of Vietnam and is written in a Latin-based script.

text: Which language serves as the working language of Ethiopia's federal government?
explanation: Amharic is the working language of Ethiopia's federal government, though the country recognises many regional languages.

text: What is the official language of Israel?
explanation: Hebrew is the official language of Israel under the country's 2018 Basic Law; Arabic holds a special status.

text: On which continent is Egypt located?
explanation: Egypt lies mainly in northeastern Africa, though the Sinai Peninsula extends into Asia.

text: Which continent is Peru located on?
explanation: Peru lies on the western coast of South America, bordering the Pacific Ocean.

text: Which continent is Mongolia located on?
explanation: Mongolia is a landlocked country in East Asia, situated between Russia and China.

text: Which continent is Fiji part of?
explanation: Fiji is an island nation in the South Pacific and is part of Oceania.

text: Which continent is Iceland part of?
explanation: Iceland is politically and culturally part of Europe, despite sitting on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

text: Which continent is Sri Lanka located on?
explanation: Sri Lanka is an island nation off the southeastern coast of India, part of South Asia.

text: Which continent is Bolivia located on?
explanation: Bolivia is a landlocked country in central South America.

text: Which continent is Madagascar part of?
explanation: Madagascar is a large island nation off the southeastern coast of Africa.

text: Which continent is Tunisia located on?
explanation: Tunisia lies on the northern coast of Africa, along the Mediterranean Sea.

text: Which continent is Costa Rica part of?
explanation: Costa Rica is in Central America, which is geographically part of the North American continent.

text: Which is the longest river in the world?
explanation: The Nile, flowing north through north-eastern Africa, is traditionally regarded as the world's longest river at roughly 6,650 km.

text: Which is the highest mountain in the world above sea level?
explanation: Mount Everest, on the Nepal-Tibet border, rises to 8,849 metres, making it the highest peak above sea level.

text: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
explanation: The Sahara, covering most of North Africa, is the world's largest hot desert at about 9.2 million square kilometres.

text: Which is the largest ocean in the world by area?
explanation: The Pacific Ocean covers more area than all the continents combined, making it the largest of the world's oceans.

text: Which is the largest lake in the world by surface area?
explanation: The Caspian Sea, bordered by five countries, is classified as a lake and is the largest inland body of water on Earth.

text: Which is the largest island in the world?
explanation: Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, is the world's largest island, as Australia is classified as a continent rather than an island.

text: Which is the largest continent by area?
explanation: Asia covers about 30% of Earth's land area, making it the largest continent by a wide margin.

text: Which is the smallest continent by landmass?
explanation: Australia is the smallest of the world's continents by total landmass.

text: Which is the largest country in the world by total area?
explanation: Russia spans roughly 17.1 million square kilometres across Europe and Asia, making it the largest country by area.

text: Which is the smallest country in the world by area?
explanation: Vatican City, an independent city-state enclosed within Rome, covers only about 0.44 square kilometres.

text: Which is the largest peninsula in the world?
explanation: The Arabian Peninsula, bordered by the Red Sea, Arabian Sea, and Persian Gulf, is the world's largest peninsula.

text: The Mariana Trench, home to the deepest known point in the world's oceans, lies in which body of water?
explanation: The Mariana Trench in the western Pacific contains the Challenger Deep, the deepest known point in any ocean.

text: Which waterfall has the world's highest uninterrupted single drop?
explanation: Angel Falls in Venezuela has an uninterrupted drop of 807 metres, the greatest of any waterfall in the world.

text: Which is the world's largest coral reef system?
explanation: The Great Barrier Reef off Australia's coast stretches over 2,300 km, making it the largest coral reef system on Earth.

text: Which is the longest mountain range on land?
explanation: The Andes run about 7,000 km along the western edge of South America, making them the longest continental mountain range.

text: Which is the largest bay in the world by area?
explanation: The Bay of Bengal, part of the northeastern Indian Ocean, is the world's largest bay by area.

text: Which is the largest gulf in the world by area?
explanation: The Gulf of Mexico, bordered by the United States, Mexico, and Cuba, is the largest gulf in the world.

text: Which country contains the world's largest archipelago?
explanation: Indonesia is made up of more than 17,000 islands, making it the largest archipelago in the world.

text: Which is the largest tropical rainforest in the world?
explanation: The Amazon Rainforest, spanning much of the Amazon Basin in South America, is the largest tropical rainforest on Earth.

text: Which city is generally regarded as the highest national capital in the world?
explanation: La Paz, Bolivia's seat of government, sits at roughly 3,640 metres above sea level, the highest elevation of any national capital.

text: Which is the world's deepest lake?
explanation: Lake Baikal in Siberia reaches a depth of about 1,642 metres, making it the deepest lake on Earth.

text: Which is the smallest of the world's oceans?
explanation: The Arctic Ocean, surrounding the North Pole, is the smallest and shallowest of the world's oceans.

text: Which is the largest river delta in the world?
explanation: The Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, spanning Bangladesh and India, is the largest river delta in the world.

text: Which country has the longest coastline in the world?
explanation: Canada's coastline, including its many islands and inlets, measures over 200,000 km, the longest of any country.

text: Which is the largest landlocked country in the world?
explanation: Kazakhstan, in Central Asia, has no coastline and is the largest landlocked country in the world by area.

text: Which is the longest man-made wall in the world?
explanation: The Great Wall of China, built and extended over centuries, stretches for thousands of kilometres across northern China.

text: Which is the world's tallest free-standing mountain, measured from base to peak?
explanation: Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania rises about 5,895 metres from its base as an isolated volcanic massif, unlike Everest which sits within a mountain range.

text: Which is the largest freshwater lake in the world by surface area?
explanation: Lake Superior, one of North America's Great Lakes, covers about 82,100 square kilometres, the largest freshwater lake by area.

text: Which plateau, often called the 'Roof of the World', is the highest and most extensive plateau on Earth?
explanation: The Tibetan Plateau, bordered by the Himalayas, has an average elevation above 4,500 metres, the highest of any large plateau.

text: Which continent is classified as the world's largest desert by area, owing to its extremely low precipitation?
explanation: By the climatological definition of a desert as a region of very low precipitation, Antarctica, covering about 14 million square kilometres, is the largest desert in the world.

text: Who is credited as the first person to reach the North Pole?
explanation: American explorer Robert Peary was recognised by the National Geographic Society and the US Congress as the first person to reach the North Pole, in 1909.

text: Who was the first person to reach the South Pole?
explanation: Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen led the first expedition to reach the South Pole, on 14 December 1911.

text: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
explanation: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface on 20 July 1969 during the Apollo 11 mission, becoming the first person to walk on the Moon.

text: Who was the first human to travel into space?
explanation: Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space when he orbited the Earth aboard Vostok 1 on 12 April 1961.

text: Who was the first woman to travel into space?
explanation: Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space when she flew aboard Vostok 6 in June 1963.

text: Who was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean?
explanation: Amelia Earhart completed a solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic in 1932, the first woman to achieve this.

text: Whose expedition was the first to circumnavigate the globe, even though he died before it was completed?
explanation: Ferdinand Magellan led the expedition that first circumnavigated the globe, but he died in the Philippines in 1521; his crew, under Juan Sebastian Elcano, completed the voyage in 1522.

text: Along with Tenzing Norgay, who was the first person to reach the summit of Mount Everest?
explanation: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay became the first climbers to reach the summit of Mount Everest, on 29 May 1953.

text: Who was the first President of the United States?
explanation: George Washington served as the first President of the United States, taking office in 1789.

text: Who was the first woman in the world to serve as a Prime Minister?
explanation: Sirimavo Bandaranaike of Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) became the world's first woman Prime Minister when she took office in 1960.

text: Which country was the first to grant women the right to vote in national elections?
explanation: New Zealand became the first self-governing country to grant women the right to vote in national elections, in 1893.

text: Who was the first person to walk in space?
explanation: Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov performed the first spacewalk in March 1965.

text: Which living creature was the first to orbit the Earth?
explanation: The Soviet dog Laika became the first living creature to orbit the Earth, aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957.

text: Along with Don Walsh, who was the first person to reach the Challenger Deep, the ocean's deepest known point?
explanation: Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh reached the bottom of the Challenger Deep in the bathyscaphe Trieste in 1960, the first to do so.

text: Which country launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite to orbit the Earth?
explanation: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 in October 1957, the first artificial satellite to orbit the Earth.

text: Which mission first landed astronauts on the Moon?
explanation: Apollo 11 carried the first crew to land on the Moon in July 1969.

text: Who was the first European explorer to reach India by an all-sea route?
explanation: Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama reached Calicut, India, by sea in 1498, opening a direct maritime route from Europe.

text: Which country was the first to test a nuclear weapon?
explanation: The United States conducted the first nuclear weapon test, code-named Trinity, in New Mexico in July 1945.

text: Who completed the first solo, nonstop transatlantic flight?
explanation: Charles Lindbergh flew the Spirit of St. Louis nonstop from New York to Paris in 1927, the first solo nonstop transatlantic flight.

text: Along with Peter Habeler, who was the first person to summit Mount Everest without supplemental oxygen?
explanation: Reinhold Messner and Peter Habeler reached the summit of Everest without bottled oxygen in 1978, a feat many had believed impossible.

text: Who was the first person to sail single-handed and nonstop around the world?
explanation: British sailor Robin Knox-Johnston completed the first solo, nonstop circumnavigation by sea in 1969.

text: Which institution is widely recognised as the oldest continually operating degree-granting university in the world?
explanation: The University of Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, founded in 859 AD, is recognised by UNESCO and Guinness World Records as the oldest existing degree-granting university.

text: Which city hosted the first modern Olympic Games?
explanation: Athens hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896, reviving the ancient Greek tradition.

text: Who was the first woman known to have circumnavigated the globe?
explanation: Jeanne Baret, a French botanist who disguised herself as a man to join Louis Antoine de Bougainville's expedition, became the first woman to circumnavigate the globe, between 1766 and 1769.

text: Who is credited with inventing the telephone?
explanation: Alexander Graham Bell was granted the first patent for the telephone in 1876 and is credited as its inventor.

text: Who is credited with developing the first practical incandescent light bulb?
explanation: Thomas Edison developed a commercially practical, long-lasting incandescent light bulb in 1879.

text: Who invented the printing press with movable metal type in Europe?
explanation: Johannes Gutenberg introduced the movable-type printing press in Europe around 1440, revolutionising the spread of printed material.

text: Which physicist developed the theory of relativity?
explanation: Albert Einstein published the special theory of relativity in 1905 and the general theory of relativity in 1915.

text: Which Scottish engineer is credited with developing the television?
explanation: John Logie Baird gave the first public demonstration of a working television system in 1926.

text: Who is credited with developing Morse code?
explanation: Samuel Morse, along with Alfred Vail, developed Morse code for use with the electric telegraph in the 1830s.

text: Who invented the World Wide Web?
explanation: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN.

text: Which Swedish chemist and engineer invented dynamite?
explanation: Alfred Nobel invented dynamite in 1867, which formed the basis of his fortune and later funded the Nobel Prizes.

text: Which Scottish bacteriologist discovered penicillin?
explanation: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 after noticing it killed bacteria in a contaminated culture dish.

text: Which brothers are credited with the first successful powered, controlled airplane flight?
explanation: Orville and Wilbur Wright achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight in December 1903.

text: Which Italian inventor is credited with pioneering long-distance radio transmission?
explanation: Guglielmo Marconi developed practical long-distance radio transmission and won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909 for this work.

text: Which English physician developed the first vaccine, against smallpox?
explanation: Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796, laying the foundation for the field of immunology.

text: Whose improvements to the steam engine made it efficient enough for widespread industrial use?
explanation: James Watt's design improvements in the 1770s greatly increased the efficiency of the steam engine, driving the Industrial Revolution.

text: Which Russian chemist created the periodic table of elements?
explanation: Dmitri Mendeleev published the periodic table of elements in 1869, arranging elements by atomic weight and properties.

text: Which naturalist proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection?
explanation: Charles Darwin proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection in his 1859 book 'On the Origin of Species'.

text: Which scientist formulated the law of universal gravitation?
explanation: Isaac Newton formulated the law of universal gravitation, published in his 1687 work 'Principia Mathematica'.

text: In which year were the first Nobel Prizes awarded?
explanation: The first Nobel Prizes, in Physics, Chemistry, Medicine, Literature, and Peace, were awarded in 1901, five years after Alfred Nobel's death.

text: The Nobel Prizes were established through the will of which Swedish inventor?
explanation: Alfred Nobel's 1895 will directed that his fortune fund annual prizes recognising achievements in several fields.

text: Who was the first person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences?
explanation: Marie Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911, the first person honoured in two different sciences.

text: Which Nobel Prize category was not part of Alfred Nobel's original 1895 will and was added later?
explanation: The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences was established by Sweden's central bank in 1968 and first awarded in 1969, decades after Nobel's original five prizes.

text: Which English engineer is known as the 'Father of Railways' for building the first successful steam locomotives?
explanation: George Stephenson built the pioneering steam locomotives Locomotion and Rocket, earning him the title 'Father of Railways'.

text: Which physicist discovered X-rays and won the first Nobel Prize in Physics?
explanation: Wilhelm Rontgen discovered X-rays in 1895 and was awarded the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 for the discovery.

text: Along with James Watson, who co-discovered the double-helix structure of DNA?
explanation: James Watson and Francis Crick proposed the double-helix structure of DNA in 1953, drawing partly on X-ray data from Rosalind Franklin.

text: Which Dutch spectacle-maker is credited with inventing the first telescope?
explanation: Hans Lippershey filed the first patent application for a telescope in 1608; Galileo later improved the design and used it for astronomy.

text: Which American virologist developed the first successful polio vaccine?
explanation: Jonas Salk developed the first successful inactivated polio vaccine, announced in 1955.
